newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia cancels controversial mining changes.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia cancels controversial mining changes.

text.p: Indonesia on Friday withdrew controversial plans to amend mining regulations, and industry representatives said the cancellation would give the sector a new momentum after the Busang debacle.
"There will be no changes. We will now go back to the COW (contracts of work) that had been initialled (last year)," Adjad Sudradjat, the director-general of mining, told Reuters.

He was speaking after chairing a 30-minute closed-door meeting with representatives from some 60 companies which had applied for the seventh-generation contracts of work for mineral mining and third-generation contracts covering the coal sector.
Adjat said the mining companies, in their response to the proposals by the government-set deadline last Tuesday, had described the changes as impractical.
"They said it would be difficult to implement. Almost all of them were not in favour because of the practicality," he said.
He declined to say if similar proposals would be included during negotiations for the next batch of contracts of work.
Adjat said the seventh-generation minerals contracts of work and the third-generation contracts for coal would be submitted to parliament for approval as soon as possible.

The contracts of work would have to be formally presented to parliament by Mines and Energy Minister Ida Bagus Sudjana, after which it would need the go ahead from President Suharto before being signed into effect by Sudjana and the mining companies.
In an immediate reaction, M. Simatupang, vice-chairman of the Indonesian Mining Association, said mining companies which applied for the contracts of work were relieved.
"They had been very concerned over the changes and had pleaded with the government not to introduce the changes and instead stick by the COW which had been initialled," he told Reuters.
"Mining companies consider the move as giving a new momentum to the industry after the Busang incident," he said.
The proposed changes included requiring mineral mining companies to allocate at least a 10-percent stake to the government for free in future ventures.

They also required mining companies with operations in Indonesia share capital gains made on stock exchanges outside the country with their shareholders and that the raising of additional capital through a public offering of shares would have to be done in Indonesia.
Some mining analysts had said the capital gains proposal would be virtually unenforceable, while Indonesia did not have the capital to finance large-scale exploration work.
Coal mining companies were, among others, required to divest 51 percent of their equity in future projects to Indonesians by the 10th year of operations.
"Everybody is relieved now that the government has decided to go forward with what it had agreed to initially," an industry executive who attended the meeting with Adjat said.
He said the government was likely to attempt to include the proposals in the next batch of contracts of work, but added that Adjat made no mention of the possibility at the meeting.
"Given the number of applicants for the COW, we could see a resurgence in exploration after the Busang scandal," he said.

Canadian exploration company Bre-X Minerals Ltd said its Busang property contained some 71 million ounces of gold, making it the biggest find this century, but an independent audit revealed the deposit was worthless.
The government declared its intention to amend mining regulations in the wake of the scandal.
